questions.question_text: Confabulation is most characteristically seen in which condition?
questions.explanation: Confabulation occurs in Korsakoff syndrome, where patients unconsciously fill memory gaps with fabricated information.

questions.question_text: Among the following options, which is accurate regarding anxiety in neurocognitive disorder?

options.text: Anxiety tends to worsen with increasing cognitive impairment.
Anxiety symptoms may be a prodrome for neurocognitive disorder even 15 years before onset of cognitive decline.
Newonset anxiety in mild cognitive impairment may indicate progression toward major neurocognitive disorder.
Anxiety is rarely seen in neurocognitive disorder.
In major neurocognitive disorder due to Alzheimer’s disease, anxiety and depression are observed but are rarely comorbid with one another.

correct_answer.text: Newonset anxiety in mild cognitive impairment may indicate progression toward major neurocognitive disorder.

questions.explanation: Newonset anxiety in mild cognitive impairment may indicate progression toward major neurocognitive disorder. Agitation, rather than anxiety, is more likely to be present as neurocognitive disorder progresses. Anxiety symptoms more than 10 years before onset of cognitive decline are consistent with a separate anxiety disorder rather than a prodrome. Anxiety is commonly observed in neurocognitive disorder and is often comorbid with depression in neurocognitive disorder due to Alzheimer’s disease. Re FeRe NCe Lenze, E. J., Mohlman, J., & Wetherell, J. L. (2015). Anxiety, obsessivecompulsive, and traumarelated disorders. In D. C. Steffens, D. G. Blazer, & M. E. Thakur (Eds.), The American Psychiatric Publishing textbook of geriatric psychiatry (5th ed., pp. 358– 359). Washington, DC: American Psychiatric Publishing. Y BoARd RevIew

questions.question_text: Hoover's sign is a clinical test used to detect:
questions.explanation: Hoover's sign assesses for non-organic weakness by observing hip extension during lower limb strength testing, with preserved strength during hip extension indicating functional weakness.

questions.question_text: What type of aura is typical for temporal lobe seizures?
questions.explanation: The most common auras in temporal lobe seizures are abdominal/epigastric sensations (described as butterflies in the stomach or a rising sensation) and psychic auras such as fear, déjà vu, or jamais vu. Auras precede temporal lobe seizures in approximately 80% of cases.

questions.question_text: Which brain lobe seizures typically produce the most formed auras?
questions.explanation: Seizures involving the temporal-parietal-occipital junction may produce more formed auras compared to seizures arising from single lobes.

questions.question_text: Wernicke's aphasia is characterized as which type of aphasia?

options.text: Global aphasia with total loss of language

questions.explanation: Wernicke's aphasia is fluent (output is fluent) but with impaired receptive/comprehension abilities.

questions.question_text: A 9yearold female child comes to the emergency room for acute headache and confusion. Exam is notable for vision loss and motor weakness. The female child has a history of recurrent headaches, recurrent vomiting, and seizures. Brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) is within normal limits. Based on history and presentation, which of the following would explain her presentation?

options.text: Mitochondrial encephalomyopathy, lactic acidosis, and strokelike episodes (MELAS) syndrome
Myoclonic epilepsy with ragged red fibers

correct_answer.text: Mitochondrial encephalomyopathy, lactic acidosis, and strokelike episodes (MELAS) syndrome

questions.explanation: MELAS syndrome is a maternally inherited mitochondrial disorder. Manifestations may include “strokelike episodes, dementia, epilepsy, lactic acidemia, myopathy, recurrent Y BOARD REvIEw headaches, hearing impairment, diabetes, and short stature” (ElHattab et al. 2015). Workup reveals lactic acidemia and ragged red fibers on muscle biopsy. Management is primarily symptomatic.

questions.question_text: Huntington's Disease - Diagnosis A 45-year-old presents with chorea, personality change, and a family history of similar symptoms. What finding confirms the diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Huntington's is confirmed by ≥36 CAG repeats in the HTT gene. MRI may show caudate atrophy but genetic testing is definitive.

questions.question_text: A 58-year-old woman post-stroke speaks fluently with normal prosody but her speech is incomprehensible with frequent paraphasias and neologisms. She cannot understand spoken or written language. Which type of aphasia is this?
questions.explanation: Wernicke's aphasia is characterized by fluent but meaningless speech with impaired comprehension.

questions.question_text: Which pathological finding is characteristic of Alzheimer's disease?
questions.explanation: Alzheimer's disease is characterized by extracellular amyloid-beta plaques and intracellular neurofibrillary tangles composed of phosphorylated tau protein.

questions.question_text: Broca's aphasia is characterized as which type of aphasia?

options.text: Non-fluent/broken speech with impaired expressive abilities

correct_answer.text: Non-fluent/broken speech with impaired expressive abilities

questions.explanation: Broca's aphasia is non-fluent/broken speech with impaired expressive abilities.

questions.question_text: A patient presents with temporal lobe atrophy, memory problems, difficulty understanding names of objects and concepts, difficulty recognizing people, and difficulty initiating movement. Which diagnosis is most likely?
questions.explanation: Semantic dementia (a variant of FTD) primarily affects the anterior temporal lobes causing loss of semantic knowledge (difficulty with names, concepts, recognition) while memory for personal events is relatively preserved, matching this clinical presentation.

questions.question_text: Which neurotransmitter system dysfunction and neuronal changes are seen in Huntington's disease?

options.text: Dopamine increase and pyramidal neuron loss
GABA reduction and medium spiny neuron loss
Serotonin excess and purkinje cell degeneration

correct_answer.text: GABA reduction and medium spiny neuron loss

questions.explanation: Huntington's disease involves dysfunction of medium spiny neurons in the striatum, with reduced GABA production, leading to the characteristic involuntary movements and cognitive decline.

questions.question_text: Among the following, which is an early symptom/sign of HIV dementia?
questions.explanation: Organic and neuropsychiatric disorders in HIV are common, and may result from the direct effects of HIV, opportunistic infections, effects of neoplasms, metabolic abnormalities, iatrogenic interventions and others. The prevalence of HIV dementia is around 10–15%. Cognitive changes may be directly due to the effects of HIV itself, secondary to opportunistic infection following treatment, or due to pre-existing psychological morbidity. These changes may be classifi ed into early and late. Early symptoms consist of forgetfulness, poor concentration, balance problems, apathy, withdrawal, dysphoric mood, and dyspraxia. Symptoms that are suggestive of a late change include disorientation, confusion, peripheral neuropathies, slowed verbal responses, indifference to illness, organic psychosis, incontinence, and carphologia (picking imaginary objects and bed linen). Lloyd G and Guthrie E. Handbook of Liaison Psychiatry, illustrated edition. Cambridge University Press, 2007, p. 482.

questions.question_text: Among the following options, which describes ataxic gait?

options.text: Stooped gait with reduced arm swing and shortened stride
Difficulty lifting feet from the ground as though the individual is held by a magnet

questions.explanation: In ataxic gait, feet are placed widely apart to maintain stability. Because of incoordination, the gait also has an uneven, unsteady, lurching pattern. 154 • PSYChIAtRY

questions.question_text: An HIVpositive, 45yearold male patient exhibits fever, headache, speech difficulties, and right hemiparesis. The individual reports that symptoms have been progressively worsening over the past few weeks. He is nonadherent with antiretroviral treatment. CD4 count is 50 cells/ μl. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) reveals multiple ringenhancing regions in the left basal ganglia and frontal cortex. Single photon emission computed tomography 162 • PSYChIAtRY (SPECT) scan demonstrates decreased uptake of thallium in these lesions. What is the best initial treatment?
questions.explanation: Cerebral toxoplasmosis is the leading cause of central nervous system (CNS) infection in acquired immunodeficiency syndrome (AIDS) that usually occurs with CD4 count less than 100 cells/ μl. Standard treatment includes a combination of sulfadiazine and pyrimethamine. Differential diagnosis includes CNS lymphoma, mycobacterial infection, bacterial abscess, progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy (PML), and others. While awaiting serology results, one can make a presumptive diagnosis of toxoplasmosis based on the clinical presentation and imaging results. In contrast to brain lymphoma, lesions in toxoplasmosis will have decreased thallium uptake on SPECT. Acyclovir and ganciclovir are used for herpes simplex encephalitis. Highdose methotrexate is effective treatment of CNS lymphoma. Finally, vancomycin and ceftriaxone are empirical treatments when bacterial meningitis is suspected.

questions.question_text: HIV-induced cognitive defi cits have been proposed to be due to
questions.explanation: All of the given mechanisms have been proposed to be the aetiopathogenesis behind cognitive defi cits in HIV infection. In the process of binding to a CD4+ receptor-containing cells, HIV gp120 binds to a calcium channel and increases intracellular free calcium. This also leads to an alteration in glucose metabolism, leading to brain dysfunction. Further, the viral genome is incorporated into the host genome, which leads to the release of more injurious compounds. These include substances such as quinolinic acid, superoxide anions, and other proinfl ammatory cytokines. These products, especially quinolinic acid, act as NMDA agonists, leading to excitotoxicity and cell death. TNF-alpha, one of the proinfl ammatory cytokines, is also known to trigger apoptosis or programmed cell death. Hales RE and Yudofsky SC. The American Psychiatric Publishing Textbook of Neuropsychiatry and Clinical Neurosciences, 4th edn. American Psychiatric Press, 2002, p. 786.

questions.question_text: Which type of aphasia is characterized by fluent but receptive language impairment?
questions.explanation: Wernicke's aphasia is a fluent aphasia with receptive language impairment, whereas Broca's aphasia is non-fluent with expressive language impairment.

questions.question_text: A 15yearold male with a learning disorder develops gradual frontal baldness and generalized stiffness of distal muscles. On examination, he has persistent contraction after percussion in his hand and leg muscles. He is not able to relax his hands after a sustained grip. Genetic testing revealed 40 repeats of CTG trinucleotide. What is the diagnosis?

options.text: Inflammatory myositis with positive muscle biopsy
A diagnosis of motor neuron disease

questions.explanation: Myotonic dystrophy is an autosomal dominant disease, caused by expansion of a CTG trinucleotide repeat in the noncoding region of DMPK. This condition usually presents in the third or fourth decade but can affect younger adults as well. Distal muscles are most involved, and patients develop frontal baldness. Patients may also have facial muscle weakness, cataracts, testicular atrophy, diabetes mellitus, and cardiac abnormality. Low IQ is often seen in this condition.

questions.question_text: In Frontotemporal Dementia, which variant is characterized by progressive impairment in motor functioning?
questions.explanation: The FTD motoric variant is characterized by progressive impairment in motor functioning with three subtypes: progressive supranuclear palsy, corticobasal degeneration, and amyotrophic lateral sclerosis.

questions.question_text: Among the following options, which medications improve muscle strength and pulmonary function in individuals with Duchenne muscle dystrophy?
questions.explanation: While gene therapy research is underway, several randomized controlled studies have suggested that prednisone has been associated with a 11% increase in muscle strength compared with placebo in Duchenne muscle dystrophy. Urine creatinine excretion, which is an indirect measure of muscle mass, is increased with prednisone treatment. Forced vital capacity (FVC) also improves significantly after 6 months of therapy with prednisone when compared with placebo. Immunosuppressant medications, including cyclosporine and azathioprine, do not improve muscle strength. Statins and zidovudine cause druginduced myopathies and have Y BOARD REvIEw no benefit in improving muscle strength in Duchenne muscle dystrophy.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is a characteristic finding in Pick's disease?
questions.explanation: Pick cells (abnormal swollen oval-shaped neuronal cells with loss of Nissl's substance and peripherally displaced nucleus) and Pick's bodies (argentophilic, tau and ubiquitin reactive filamentous inclusions) are pathological hallmarks of Pick's disease.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is a characteristic histopathological finding in Alzheimer's disease?

options.text: Pick bodies and Pick cells only
Neurofibrillary tangles, senile plaques, Hirano bodies, and neuronal loss
Lewy bodies in the temporal lobes

correct_answer.text: Neurofibrillary tangles, senile plaques, Hirano bodies, and neuronal loss

questions.explanation: Alzheimer's disease is characterized by neurofibrillary tangles (hyperphosphorylated tau protein), senile plaques (insoluble amyloid peptide deposits that are eosinophilic), Hirano bodies, and neuronal and synaptic loss, along with granulovascular degeneration and glial activation.

questions.question_text: A chronic alcoholic is telling stories with no link between events. What phenomenon occurs in confabulation?
questions.explanation: Confabulation involves unconscious filling in of memory gaps with fabricated information. The person genuinely believes these false memories, often with autobiographical content that lacks logical connections or temporal accuracy.

questions.question_text: Global aphasia is distinguished by

options.text: Impaired comprehension but intact repetition and naming
Fluent speech with intact comprehension and repetition
Intact comprehension with impaired naming and fluency
Impaired comprehension with intact comprehension of repetition

questions.explanation: Global aphasia, which results from extensive dominanthemispheric damage, causes an extreme form of nonfluent aphasia in which patients have impaired comprehension, expression, repetition, and naming. Patients often become mute and present with right hemiplegia, right homonymous hemianopsia, and conjugate deviation of eyes to the left.

questions.question_text: A 35-year-old man sustained a severe traumatic brain injury in a road traffic accident 6 months ago. He has made good physical recovery but his wife reports new onset of impulsivity, inattention, and difficulty organizing tasks. Which psychiatric condition is he most likely experiencing as a sequela?
questions.explanation: ADHD is a recognized neuropsychiatric sequela of traumatic brain injury.

questions.question_text: A 51yearold white male patient with previous cervical spinal arthritis reports increasing pain in the neck and bilateral shoulders. Three months ago he was in an automobile accident in which he was a restrained passenger, and immediate cervical spine MRI at the time revealed no changes from his previous study. On examination, he has deltoid wasting bilaterally and reduced pinprick and temperature sensation over both shoulders and neck. Sensation to light touch is preserved. 150 • PSYChIAtRY A repeat MRI of the cervical spine at this time is likely to reveal which of the following conditions?
questions.explanation: The above case describes presentation consistent with syringomyelia developing a few months after a traumatic injury. Syringomyelia can also develop several years after the initial trauma. It presents with impaired pinprick and temperature sensation with preserved light touch sensation in a “capelike” fashion over neck and shoulders. Affected individuals often report diffuse neck pain and radicular pain in both arms. MRI of the cervical spine shows focal spinal cord enlargement at the level of the lesion in traumatic cases.

questions.question_text: Which type of memory is typically preserved in schizophrenia?
questions.explanation: While schizophrenia is associated with broad cognitive deficits including impaired attention, working memory, episodic memory, and processing speed, procedural memory and semantic memory tend to be relatively preserved.

questions.question_text: In a patient with mild neurocognitive disorder (NCD), which of the following would distinguish probable from possible Alzheimer’s disease?

options.text: Evidence of a causative Alzheimer’s disease genetic mutation from either genetic testing or family history.
Clear evidence of decline in memory and learning.
Steadily progressive, gradual decline in cognition, without extended plateaus.
A diagnosis of presence of APOE e4 allele.

correct_answer.text: Evidence of a causative Alzheimer’s disease genetic mutation from either genetic testing or family history.

questions.explanation: The only way that mild NCD due to probable Alzheimer’s disease can be diagnosed is if there is evidence of a causative Alzheimer’s disease genetic mutation from either genetic testing or family history. Mild NCD due to possible Alzheimer’s disease is diagnosed on the basis of the presence of all of the clinical criteria described in options B–D above. Age at onset is not a diagnostic criterion.

questions.question_text: Among the following, which is the most significant factor in increasing the risk of suicide in epilepsy?

options.text: Frequent medication changes and poor drug compliance

questions.explanation: Suicide is increased fi vefold among patients with epilepsy. Among patients presenting with self-harm, epileptic subjects are over-represented from fi ve- to sevenfold. Risk factors for suicide in epilepsy are ranked as follows: (1) Comorbid psychiatric disorders (2) relatively young males (ages 25–49 years); (3) temporal lobe seizures (with brain lesions); (4) prolonged duration of the seizure disorder (5) inadequate therapy (6) personal, social, or occupational diffi culties; and (7) availability of large amounts of antiepileptic drugs. Trimble M and Schmitz B. The Neuropsychiatry of Epilepsy. Cambridge University Press, 2002, p. 108.

questions.question_text: FTD - tau and ubiquitin status in familial FTD
questions.explanation: In familial FTD, the pattern is typically tau-negative and ubiquitin-positive. Pick's disease (a form of FTD) is tau-positive and ubiquitin-positive. Overall, the most common pattern in FTD is ubiquitin-positive and amyloid-negative.

questions.question_text: A patient presents with apathy, restricted dietary habits, agitation, and emotional lability. Which diagnosis is most likely?
questions.explanation: Apathy, behavioral changes (agitation, emotional lability), and dietary habit changes are characteristic features of behavioral variant frontotemporal dementia (bvFTD).

questions.question_text: Which type of seizure aura is most common in temporal lobe epilepsy?
questions.explanation: Autonomic aura is the most common type of aura in temporal lobe seizures, causing epigastric sensations, salivation, and sometimes vertigo.

questions.question_text: Which medication is used to treat motor symptoms in Huntington's disease?
questions.explanation: Tetrabenazine, a vesicular monoamine transporter inhibitor, is used to treat the involuntary movements (chorea) associated with Huntington's disease.

questions.question_text: What is the characteristic frequency of tremor in Parkinson's disease?
questions.explanation: The tremor characteristic of Parkinson's disease occurs at a frequency of 4-6 Hz (approximately 5 Hz), which is a classic diagnostic feature of the condition.

questions.question_text: Which is a human prion disease?

options.text: Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease and Fatal Familial Insomnia

correct_answer.text: Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease and Fatal Familial Insomnia

questions.explanation: Fatal Familial Insomnia and Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease are both human prion diseases; they are caused by misfolded prion proteins.

questions.question_text: A man had a motor vehicle accident 5 years ago. He now presents with bilateral coarse tremors and impaired eye focusing (reduced gaze). Sleeping tablets improved his tremors. Which diagnosis is most likely?
questions.explanation: While the 5-year timeline makes post-concussional syndrome less likely (symptoms typically appear earlier), and adjustment disorder is less probable given the specific neurological symptoms, PTSD with associated motor manifestations could present this way. However, the specific combination of tremor and gaze disturbance responding to sedation suggests a functional rather than organic neurological cause.

questions.question_text: In Parkinson's disease, what is the typical frequency of the resting tremor?
questions.explanation: The resting tremor in Parkinson's disease typically has a frequency of 4-6 Hz (approximately 5 Hz).

questions.question_text: The pulvinar sign on neuroimaging is characteristic of
questions.explanation: The pulvinar sign (bilateral high signal in the pulvinar and anterior basal ganglia on MRI) is characteristic of variant Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease (vCJD).

questions.question_text: CLINICAL ASPECtS OF N EUR
questions.explanation: The essential feature of insomnia disorder is characterized by dissatisfaction with sleep quantity or quality with complaints of difficulty of initiating or maintaining sleep. The sleep complaints must cause clinically significant distress or impairment in social, occupational, or other important areas of functioning. The sleep disturbance may occur during the course of another mental or medical disorder, or it may occur independently.

questions.question_text: An 83yearold male patient comes to the emergency room for confusion and falls. Assessment of gait is suggestive of apraxia. His partner notes that he has been increasingly incontinent of urine for several weeks. Computerized tomography (CT) scan of the head demonstrates enlarged ventricles. What surgical procedure may be helpful for this individual?

options.text: Pallidotomy of the left globus pallidus
Shunt placement into the lateral ventricle

correct_answer.text: Shunt placement into the lateral ventricle

questions.explanation: This patient presents with the clinical triad of gait apraxia, urinary incontinence, and dementia, classically associated with normal pressure hydrocephalus (NPH). Typically patients undergo serial lumbar puncture to decrease the degree of hydrocephalus and may show some improvement with this intervention alone. For longterm treatment, neurosurgery involving shunt placement into the lateral ventricle is considered.

questions.question_text: A 78yearold male patient exhibits unilateral hand tremor for 3 months. On exam, he is observed to have a short, shuffling stride and a positive “pull test.” His posture is stooped. He is slow to initiate movement. Which of the following symptoms would NOT be expected in someone with his likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: This patient likely carries a diagnosis of Parkinson disease (historically “paralysis agitans”). Classic presentation includes tremor, rigidity, akinesia/ bradykinesia, and postural instability (easily remembered by the acronym TRAP). The “pull test” is a measure of postural instability. Associated symptoms may include micrographia, hypophonia, masked facies, autonomic dysfunction, anosmia, dysphagia, and multiple neuropsychiatric complications (cognitive decline, depression, sleep disorder, or psychosis).

questions.question_text: A young, healthy female patient exhibits mental status changes, including confusion, autonomic instability, choreathetoid movements, seizures, agitation, and bizarre hallucinations. Routine medical workup including CSF examination is significant for lymphocytic pleocytosis, and a brain MRI reveals no acute findings. Viral and bacterial cultures are negative. A few days after the individual has been admitted to the ICU, you are informed that CSF assay for anti– NMDA receptor antibodies returned positive. Which of the following will determine the overall clinical outlook of this condition is good?

options.text: Early tumor detection, removal, and immunosuppression

correct_answer.text: Early tumor detection, removal, and immunosuppression

questions.explanation: The above case describes the clinical presentation of anti– NMDA receptor encephalitis. This condition belongs to a group of autoimmune encephalitides. When this condition is associated with teratoma, early detection and removal of the tumor and treatment with 13. mANAGEmENt AND tREA tmENt immunosuppressants portend a favorable outcome. In many cases of antiNMDA receptor encephalitis, no tumor can be found. As these antibodies are directly pathogenic by activating NMDA receptors, immunosuppression is firstline management. Other autoimmune encephalitides, such as paraneoplastic meningoencephalitis associated with antiHu antibodies, have unfavorable outcomes both because of the associated malignancy and because immunosuppression is largely ineffective. Antibodies such as antiHu target intracellular epitopes, and neurological symptoms are due principally to cytotoxic (T8) cell effects.

questions.question_text: The essential feature of the DSM-5 diagnosis of delirium is a disturbance in attention/awareness and in cognition that develops over a short period of time, represents a change from baseline, and tends to fluctuate in severity during the course of a day. which of the following options additional conditions must apply?

options.text: There must be laboratory evidence of an evolving dementia.
The disturbance must develop as a direct result of a medical condition or substance.
The disturbance must not occur in the context of a severely reduced level of arousal, such as coma.
The disturbance must be a direct physiological consequence of a substance use disorder.
The disturbance must not be superimposed on a preexisting neurocognitive disorder.

correct_answer.text: The disturbance must not occur in the context of a severely reduced level of arousal, such as coma.

questions.explanation: The essential feature of delirium is a disturbance of attention or awareness (Criterion A) that is accompanied by a change in baseline cognition (Criterion C) that cannot be better explained by a preexisting or evolving neurocognitive disorder (Criterion D1). The ability to evaluate cognition to diagnose delirium depends on there being a level of arousal sufficient for response to verbal stimulation; hence, delirium should not be diagnosed in the context of coma (Criterion D2). The disturbance develops over a short period of time, usually hours to a few days, and tends to fluctuate during the course of the day (Criterion B). There is evidence from the history, physical examination, or laboratory findings that the disturbance is a physiological consequence of an underlying medical condition, substance intoxication or withdrawal, use of a medication, or a toxin exposure, or a combination of these factors (Criterion E). Both major and mild neurocognitive disorders (NCDs) can increase the risk for delirium and complicate the course. The most common differential diagnostic issue when evaluating confusion in older adults is disentangling symptoms of delirium and dementia. The clinician must determine whether the individual has delirium; a delirium superimposed on a preexisting NCD, such as that due to Alzheimer’s disease; or an NCD without delirium. The traditional distinction between delirium and dementia according to acuteness of onset and temporal course is particularly difficult in those elderly individuals 406 | Neurocognitive Disorders—ANSWER GUIDE who had a prior NCD that may not have been recognized, or who develop persistent cognitive impairment following an episode of delirium.

questions.question_text: Wernicke's aphasia is characterized by which type of speech output?
questions.explanation: Wernicke's aphasia is characterized by fluent speech that lacks coherence and meaning (fluent aphasia with impaired comprehension).

questions.question_text: A 38yearold male patient exhibits subacute onset of lower extremity weakness accompanied by a “pins and needles” sensation. He reported that 2 weeks ago he experienced abdominal cramping, periumbilical pain, and diarrhea. He has no significant prior medical history. On physical examination there was diffuse muscle weakness in all four extremities with distal weakness greater than proximal. Muscle tone was decreased, and reflexes were absent. Which of the following is firstline clinical approach?
questions.explanation: Weakness with loss of reflexes is suggestive of lower motor neuron lesion. Guillain– Barré syndrome is an acute illness that usually follows an infection. Plasmapheresis and intravenous immune globulin are effective by eliminating antimyelin and antiaxonal antibodies. Immunomodulatory agents, as well as supportive care including respiratory and cardiovascular management, are mainstays of treatment. Corticosteroids are typically not beneficial and so are not generally recommended. t OF NEUROLOGICAL DISORDERS • 161

questions.question_text: Which of the following is not a form of frontotemporal dementia?
questions.explanation: Huntington's disease typically affects the basal ganglia in the early phases of the disorder but then generally spreads to affect all cortical areas. Progressive supranuclear palsy was thought to be related to Parkinson's disease but is now thought to be more related to frontotemporal dementia. Pick's disease, progressive non-fluent aphasia, and semantic dementia are all recognized forms of frontotemporal dementia.

questions.question_text: Which histopathological finding in Alzheimer's disease consists of extracellular, insoluble amyloid peptide deposits appearing apple green?
questions.explanation: Senile plaques are extracellular, insoluble amyloid peptide deposits that appear eosinophilic and stain apple green with special staining techniques. They are characteristic of Alzheimer's disease pathology.

questions.question_text: Seizures originating in the parietal lobe typically begin with which type of aura?

options.text: Visual aura with colored lines or spots

questions.explanation: Parietal lobe seizures characteristically begin with a contralateral somatosensory aura, typically of the positive type such as electrical sensations or tingling, reflecting the location of the sensory cortex in this region.

questions.question_text: Which protein inclusion profile is most common in familial FTD?
questions.explanation: Familial FTD is characterized by tau-negative but ubiquitin-positive neuronal cytoplasmic inclusions, often due to mutations in the PGRN gene on chromosome 17q21. In contrast, Pick's disease (a type of FTD) shows tau-positive, ubiquitin-positive inclusions. Most common general FTD profile is ubiquitin positive with amyloid negative.

questions.question_text: A neuropsychiatrist assesses prognostic factors after traumatic brain injury. Which is the best predictor of outcome after TBI?
questions.explanation: Post-traumatic amnesia (PTA) duration is the best predictor of cognitive outcome after TBI. Longer PTA = worse prognosis.

questions.question_text: Among the following options, which features best differentiates delirium from major neurocognitive disorder?
questions.explanation: Inattention is required for a diagnosis of delirium. DSM5 has introduced the specifiers hyperactive, hypoactive, and mixed level of activity, but these are not required for delirium diagnosis. Re FeRe NCe American Psychiatric Association. (2013). Diagnostic and statistical manual of mental disorders (5th ed.). Arlington, VA: American Psychiatric Publishing.

questions.question_text: Which neurotransmitter abnormality is identified most consistently in delirium?
questions.explanation: There is evidence that cholinergic deficiency plays a role in delirium. Increased dopaminergic activity may also play a role. The roles of serotonin, glutamate, and GABA in delirium are less well established. Re FeRe NCe Solai, L. K. K. (2009). Delirium. In B. J. Sadock, V. A. Sadock & P. Ruiz (Eds.), Kaplan and Sadock’s comprehensive textbook of psychiatry (9th ed., p. 1157). Philadelphia, PA: Wolters Kluwer Health/ Lippincott Williams and Wilkins.

questions.question_text: In Wernicke's aphasia, which language function remains relatively intact?
questions.explanation: Wernicke's aphasia is characterized by relatively preserved fluency with impaired comprehension, unlike Broca's aphasia where fluency is reduced but comprehension remains more intact.

questions.question_text: Excessive startle response occurs in which condition?
questions.explanation: Hyperekplexia is a condition characterized by excessive startle response to sudden, unexpected stimuli. It is an exaggerated reflex response to acoustic or tactile stimulation.

questions.question_text: Pick's disease is characterized by which of the following pathological features?
questions.explanation: Pick's disease is characterized by both Tau positivity and Ubiquitin positivity. Familial FTD is typically Tau negative and Ubiquitin positive, while most FTD cases are Ubiquitin positive and Amyloid negative.

questions.question_text: Differentiating Dementia from Normal Aging A 74-year-old patient has memory concerns. You want to distinguish pathological changes from normal aging. Which feature suggests dementia rather than normal aging?

options.text: Forgetting the day then remembering later

questions.explanation: Personality and behavioral changes (apathy, disinhibition, fixed irritability) suggest pathological process. Minor memory lapses with retrieval can be normal aging.

questions.question_text: Psychosis in Parkinson's Disease A patient with Parkinson's disease develops psychotic symptoms. Medical causes have been excluded. Which antipsychotic has the best evidence in PD psychosis?
questions.explanation: Clozapine and quetiapine have the lowest risk of worsening motor symptoms. Clozapine has the best evidence but requires monitoring.

questions.question_text: Among the following, which is a monogenic ischaemic stroke syndrome?

options.text: A diagnosis of moya Moya disease

questions.explanation: CADASIL (cerebral autosomal dominant arteriopathy with subcortical infarcts and leucoencephalopathy) is an autosomal dominant familial trait linked in several families to a mutation in the Notch 3 gene on chromosome 19. It presents as recurrent small-vessel strokes, beginning in early adulthood, leading to extensive symmetric white matter changes similar to Binswanger’s disease and progressive dementia. The genetic nature of the syndrome may not be fully apparent because of the low penetrance. Approximately 40% of patients have migraine with aura. CADASIL is the only monogenic ischaemic stroke syndrome described. Genetic testing is available. Kasper DL, et al. Harrison’s Principles of Internal Medicine. McGraw-Hill, 2005.

questions.question_text: In the ABC model of apathy seen in dementia, the core deficit is characterized by a profound lack of...
questions.explanation: The ABC (Affective, Behavioral, Cognitive) model categorizes apathy, but no matter how it is characterized, there is a consensus that a lack of motivation is at the core of apathy.

questions.question_text: Among the following options, which are risk factors for the development of delirium? (Check all that apply.)

options.text: Visual impairment F. Elevated albumin G. Elevated BUN

questions.explanation: LL BUT F Advanced age, neurocognitive impairment, polypharmacy, functional impairment, visual impairment, low albumin, and elevated BUN have all been identified as risk factors for developing delirium.

questions.question_text: Which protein pathology is most commonly found in frontotemporal dementia?

options.text: Ubiquitin and tau positive, amyloid negative
All three pathologies in equal amounts

correct_answer.text: Ubiquitin and tau positive, amyloid negative

questions.explanation: Frontotemporal dementia is most commonly associated with ubiquitin-positive and amyloid-negative pathology, followed by tau-positive and amyloid-negative, with Pick's disease showing both tau and ubiquitin positivity.

questions.question_text: A 65-year-old man post-stroke has difficulty finding the right words during conversation. His speech is fluent and grammatically correct, but he frequently pauses searching for specific words. Comprehension and repetition are intact. Which type of aphasia is this?
questions.explanation: Anomic aphasia presents with word-finding difficulty while preserving fluency, comprehension, and repetition.

questions.question_text: Which feature is accepted as a core feature of Lewy body dementia?
questions.explanation: Visual hallucinations are a core diagnostic feature of Lewy body dementia, occurring in the majority of cases and often an early symptom.

questions.question_text: You are evaluating an 18yearold female individual with worsening academic performance, depression, and irritability. On interview you note dysarthria, drooling, and wingbeating tremor. What would be the next best step in the clinical approach of this individual?

options.text: Start SSRI because the individual is depressed.
Pursue CT scan of the brain.
Start stimulant for attention deficit hyperactivity disorder.
Pursue laboratory work and refer the individual to ophthalmology for slitlamp examination.

correct_answer.text: Pursue laboratory work and refer the individual to ophthalmology for slitlamp examination.

questions.explanation: Wilson’s disease is suspected when a young patient presents with a variety of neurological and psychiatric symptoms. Wilson’s disease is inherited in an autosomal recessive manner, so obtaining a family history is helpful. This is specifically the case in the beginning of the illness when liver failure is not apparent. Symptoms of Wilson’s disease include liver disease (most often with elevated aminotransferase levels, jaundice, and abdominal pain), as well as neurological (dysarthria, dysphagia, tremors, dystonia) and psychiatric (depression, personality change, irritability) symptoms. Among all the symptoms described above, presence of wing-b eating tremor is specific for Wilson’s disease. Finally, given suspicion of Wilson’s disease, the next step in management should be referral for ophthalmologic exam (Kayser– Fleischer rings) and labs (serum ceruloplasmin, 24hour urinary copper excretion, liver function tests).

questions.question_text: Among the following options, which statements is Accurate regarding depression in cancer individuals?

options.text: death rate is unaffected by the presence of depression in cancer individuals.
Terminally ill cancer individuals who wish death would come quickly are no more likely to be depressed than individuals who do not wish to die.
Depression is an expected reaction to a cancer diagnosis and does not need treatment.
Depression in cancer individuals is highly associated with physical functioning.
Depression rates are comparable for cancer individuals in inpatient and outpatient settings.

correct_answer.text: Depression in cancer individuals is highly associated with physical functioning.

questions.explanation: Patients with cancer who are the most physically disabled have significantly higher rates of major depressive disorder than those who are moderately disabled or in good physical condition. The presence of depression increases mortality in cancer patients. Patients who wish death would come quickly are more likely to be depressed than those who do

questions.question_text: Among the following options, which diseases of the endocrine system has been linked to onset of depression?
questions.explanation: All of the above endocrine disorders have been associated with onset of depression. Y BoARd RevIew Re FeRe NCe Akiskal, H. S. (2009). Mood disorders: Clinical features. In B. J. Sadock, V. A. Sadock, & P. Ruiz (Eds.), Kaplan and Sadock’s comprehensive textbook of psychiatry (9th ed., p. 1727). Philadelphia, PA: Wolters Kluwer Health/ Lippincott Williams and Wilkins.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is a human prion disease?
questions.explanation: All of these are human prion diseases, along with kuru, which are transmissible spongiform encephalopathies.

questions.question_text: What is the typical aura experienced by patients with parietal lobe seizures?

options.text: Somatosensory disturbances including body image distortion

correct_answer.text: Somatosensory disturbances including body image distortion

questions.explanation: Parietal lobe seizures typically begin with contralateral somatosensory auras including tingling, electrical sensations, and body image distortion (hyperschemazia), often with positive sensory phenomena.

questions.question_text: Which of the following describes locked-in syndrome?

options.text: Complete loss of consciousness with preserved brainstem reflexes
Inability to speak due to motor cortex damage
Total paralysis below the level of the third nerve nuclei with ability to open eyes voluntarily and move eyes vertically
Loss of all eye movements with preserved limb function

correct_answer.text: Total paralysis below the level of the third nerve nuclei with ability to open eyes voluntarily and move eyes vertically

questions.explanation: Locked-in syndrome results from ventral pontine lesions and describes total paralysis below the level of the third nerve nuclei, but patients can open their eyes voluntarily and elevate or depress their eyes to command, while horizontal eye movements are usually lost.

questions.question_text: Among the following options, which has been shown to prevent HIVassociated neurocognitive disorder?

options.text: Antiretroviral treatment with high CNS penetration

questions.explanation: There is no question that combined antiretroviral therapy (cART; historically highly active antiretroviral therapy, or HAART) has transformed HIV from a death sentence to a chronic disease, and severe dementia due to HIV disease itself (likely an immunemediated process) has given way to milder forms of neurocognitive impairment. In this way, cART has influenced the course and severity of HAND. It has not eliminated it though. Up to half of patients still have significant neurocognitive impairment. There is no clear evidence that cART regimens with high CNS penetration prevent HAND, though highpenetration regimens are generally recommended to lower HIV concentration in the cerebrospinal fluid. Psychostimulants may be used to treat symptoms of y BoARd REVIEw HAND such as slowed processing speed but do not alter the disease course.

questions.question_text: FTD - Aphasia Type A patient with behavioral variant FTD also has progressive language difficulties. Which type of aphasia is most commonly associated with FTD?
questions.explanation: Progressive non-fluent aphasia (PNFA) is an FTD variant with effortful, non-fluent speech and agrammatism.

questions.question_text: A 69-year-old semiretired radiologist with responsibility for chest x-ray interpretation at his academic medical center has been referred by the hospital’s Employee Assistance Program for clinical evaluation because of concerns expressed by other clinicians that he has been making many mistakes in his x-ray interpretations over the past few months. Evaluation discloses a remote prior diagnosis of alcohol dependence with sobriety for the past 20 years, and a depressive episode following the death of his wife 9 years before the current problem, treated with cognitive-behavioral therapy with full resolution of symptoms after 6 months and no recurrence. He acknowledges some trouble concentrating but no other symptoms, and he minimizes the alleged x-ray interpretation problems. He cannot state the correct date or day of the week and cannot recall the previous day’s news events, but he can describe highlights of his long career in medicine in great detail. Collateral history from his children reveals that on several occasions in the past year neighbors in his apartment building had complained that he forgot to turn off his stove while cooking, resulting in a smoke-filled apartment. He scores 21/30 on the Mini-Mental State Examination. What diagnosis most accurately describes this clinical picture?

options.text: A diagnosis of major neurocognitive disorder (NCD).
A diagnosis of mild neurocognitive disorder.
A diagnosis of major depressive disorder.
A diagnosis of adjustment disorder with mixed disturbance of emotions and conduct.

correct_answer.text: A diagnosis of major neurocognitive disorder (NCD).

questions.explanation: Concern has been raised about cognitive decline affecting this patient’s functioning, and his test performance is very abnormal, so he clearly meets Criterion A for major NCD. Forgetting to keep track of what is cooking on the stovetop, with the result that neighbors have to intervene because of a smoke condition, is a good example of inability to perform activities of daily living independently, so he meets Criterion B for major NCD, as opposed to mild NCD. He is not delirious, so he meets Criterion C. Neither his remote history of alcohol dependence nor his remote history of depression accounts for his cognitive problems, and there is no evidence of another mental disorder, so he probably also meets Criterion D.

questions.question_text: Among the following options, which is inaccurate of individuals who develop alcoholrelated dementia (ARD)?
questions.explanation: Individuals who develop ARD are predominantly male, have comorbid psychiatric and medical conditions (including liver and digestive diseases), are socially isolated, and are often identified through hospital admissions.

questions.question_text: A 68-year-old semiretired cardiologist with responsibility for electrocardiogram (ECG) interpretation at his community hospital is referred by the hospital’s Employee Assistance Program for clinical evaluation because of concerns expressed by other clinicians that he has been making many mistakes in his ECG interpretations over the past few months. The patient discloses symptoms of persistent sadness since the death of his wife 6 months prior to the evaluation, with frequent thoughts of death, trouble sleeping, and escalating usage of sedative-hypnotics and alcohol. He has some trouble concentrating, but he has been able to maintain his household, pay his bills, shop, and prepare meals by himself without difficulty. He scores 28/30 on the Mini-Mental State Examination (MMSE). which of the following options would be the primary consideration in the differential diagnosis?

options.text: A diagnosis of major neurocognitive disorder due to Alzheimer's disease.
A diagnosis of mild neurocognitive disorder.
A diagnosis of adjustment disorder with depressed mood.
A diagnosis of major depressive disorder.

correct_answer.text: A diagnosis of major depressive disorder.

questions.explanation: Not enough information has been provided to know for certain whether this patient meets criteria for a specific mood disorder diagnosis—or for a substance use disorder diagnosis—but a major NCD can be ruled out. Although the patient’s test score on the MMSE is within the normal range, he does meet Criterion A for major NCD, in that concerns about a decline in cognitive function have been raised due to his increased error rate in interpreting ECGs. Regarding Criterion B for major NCD, the patient does not demonstrate loss of ability to perform activities of daily living independently and so does not qualify for a diagnosis of major NCD. He does meet Criterion C, in that he is not demonstrating signs of delirium. The fact that his problems have become evident only in the context of mood issues strongly suggests that a depressive disorder and/or substance use may account for his work performance deficits; therefore, he likely will not meet Criterion D for NCD. Although he could meet Criterion B for mild NCD, a mood disorder would be the most prominent consideration in the differential diagnosis.

questions.question_text: Loss of the striatum is characteristic of which neurodegenerative disorder?
questions.explanation: Huntington's disease involves selective degeneration of the striatum, particularly the caudate nucleus and putamen, leading to characteristic motor symptoms.

questions.question_text: Among the following options, which is not a predisposing factor for major and mild neurocognitive disorder due to HIV infection?

options.text: Longterm use of combined antiretroviral treatment

correct_answer.text: Longterm use of combined antiretroviral treatment

questions.explanation: Combined antiretroviral therapy (cART; historically “highly active antiretroviral therapy,” or HAART) improves cognitive function in patients experiencing neurocognitive disorder due to HIV infection. Comorbid cytomegalovirus or toxoplasmosis may worsen cognition, as do comorbid hepatitis C infection and general vascular risk factors.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is NOT a type of fronto-temporal degeneration (FTD)?
questions.explanation: Huntington's disease is not a type of FTD. The five clinical subtypes of FTD are: behavioral variant FTD, primary progressive aphasia (Pick's disease), progressive non-fluent aphasia, semantic dementia, and logopenic progressive aphasia. PSP (progressive supranuclear palsy) was previously classified under FTD but is now classified as Atypical Parkinsonism in ICD-11.

questions.question_text: What is the primary pathological hallmark of Lewy body dementia?
questions.explanation: Alpha-synuclein accumulation in the temporal lobe, cingulate gyrus, frontal lobes and dorsal motor nucleus of the vagus characterizes Lewy body dementia, forming Lewy bodies which are weakly eosinophilic, spherical, cytoplasmic inclusions.

questions.question_text: Braak stages are used in neuropathological quantifi cation of brain changes in Alzheimer’s disease. Which of the following is the basis of Braak’s stages?
questions.explanation: Braak’s staging system has been used to grade pathologically the various degrees of dementia severity. It is based on the appearance of neurofi brillary tangles in brain. These tangles commence the transentorhinal and entorhinal cortex spreading to the hippocampus, and then extend across the remaining limbic system before involving other cortical regions, followed by the primary motor and somatosensory cortices, and fi nally the occipital cortex. This progression is the basis of the Braak’s staging. A decline in memory test performance and mental state of the demented patient correlate with the pathological progression through the neocortical Braak stages. Gelder MG, et al., eds. Shorter Oxford Textbook of Psychiatry, 5th edn. Oxford University Press, 2006, p. 337.

questions.question_text: A 54yearold male patient comes to a neurologist for evaluation of weakness. The neurologist observes muscle fasciculation and atrophy. Exam is notable for brisk deep tendon reflexes and positive Babinski sign. Electromyography shows fibrillation potentials and positive sharp waves. Which of the following agents is approved by the FDA for this illness?
questions.explanation: This patient likely has amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS), as evidenced by presentation of upper motor neuron signs (e.g., brisk deep tendon reflexes, positive Babinski sign) and lower motor neuron signs (e.g., muscle fasciculation, positive sharp waves/ fibrillation potentials on electromyography). Riluzole is an inhibitor of glutamate release and is used for treatment of ALS, increasing life expectancy by 3 to 6 months.

questions.question_text: Which of the following protein inclusion profiles is most common in FTD?
questions.explanation: FTD classification is based on protein inclusions: tau, TDP-43, and FUS. The most common profile in FTD generally is ubiquitin positive with amyloid negative, followed by tau positive with amyloid negative. Atypical FTD with ubiquitin-positive inclusions is relatively rare and characterized by FUS-positive inclusions.

questions.question_text: In the fifth edition of the Diagnostic and Statistic Manual of Mental Disorders (DSM5), neurocognitive impairment is now classified as mild or major neurocognitive disorder. What is an significant distinction between these two categories?

options.text: Major neurocognitive disorder must have an identified genetic etiology.
Deficits of mild neurocognitive disorder do not interfere with daily activities.
Major neurocognitive disorder requires only subjective concerns without objective testing.
Major neurocognitive disorder has acute onset whereas mild neurocognitive disorder is insidious.
Behavioral disturbances are observed only in major neurocognitive disorder.

correct_answer.text: Deficits of mild neurocognitive disorder do not interfere with daily activities.

questions.explanation: One of the key distinctions between mild and major neurocognitive disorders in DSM5 is that patients with mild neurocognitive disorder do not have deficits that interfere with daily activities. Another distinction is that although patients with both conditions have some decline from their previous level of functioning, this decline is modest in mild neurocognitive disorder and significant in major

questions.question_text: Which of the following brain changes is NOT typically seen in adults with a history of childhood abuse?
questions.explanation: Childhood abuse is associated with reduced size of the amygdala, hippocampus, and anterior cingulate cortex, along with altered stress response. Adults with a history of childhood abuse typically show reduced prefrontal cortex size, not increased size.

questions.question_text: Confabulation is most commonly seen in which condition?
questions.explanation: Confabulation is most commonly seen in Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome, where it occurs in clear consciousness as falsification of memory, along with other conditions like Alzheimer's disease and traumatic brain injury.

questions.question_text: Major or mild neurocognitive disorder (NCD) due to prion disease encompasses NCDs linked to a group of subacute spongiform encephalopathies caused by transmissible agents known as prions. What is the most common prion disease?

options.text: A diagnosis of bovine spongiform encephalopathy.

questions.explanation: Prion diseases include Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease, variant Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease, kuru, Gerstmann-Sträussler-Scheinker syndrome, and fatal insomnia. The most common type is sporadic Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease, typically referred to as Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease (CJD). (Variant CJD is much rarer and is associated with transmission of bovine spongiform encephalopathy, also called “mad cow disease.”) Typically, individuals with CJD present with neurocognitive deficits, ataxia, and abnormal movements such as myoclonus, chorea, or dystonia; a startle reflex is also common. Typically, the history reveals rapid progression to major NCD over as little as 6 months, and thus the disorder is typically seen only at the major level. However, many individuals with the disorder may have atypical presentations, and the disease can be confirmed only by biopsy or at autopsy. Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome, neurosyphilis, and Huntington’s disease are not prion diseases; rather, Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome is secondary to thiamine deficiency, Huntington’s disease is secondary to a genetic defect, and neurosyphilis is caused by a sexually transmitted infection.

questions.question_text: A neurologist reviews causes of cognitive decline that are not primarily neurodegenerative. Which is a non-degenerative cause of neurocognitive disorder?
questions.explanation: Multiple sclerosis causes cognitive impairment through inflammatory demyelination, not neurodegeneration.

questions.question_text: The diagnostic criteria for neurocognitive disorder (NCD) due to HIV infection encompasses fulfillment of criteria for major or mild NCD and documented infection with human immunodeficiency virus (as established through established laboratory methods). which of the following options is a prominent feature of NCD due to HIV infection?

options.text: A diagnosis of impairment in executive functioning.
A diagnosis of marked personality change.
Significant delusions and hallucinations at onset of the disorder.
Marked difficulty with recall of learned information.
Rapid progression to profound neurocognitive impairment.

correct_answer.text: A diagnosis of impairment in executive functioning.

questions.explanation: NCD associated with HIV infection generally shows a “subcortical pattern” with prominently impaired executive function, slowing of pro410 | Neurocognitive Disorders—ANSWER GUIDE cessing speed, problems with more demanding attentional tasks, and difficulty in learning new information, but fewer problems with recall of learned information. In major NCD, slowing may be prominent. Language difficulties, such as aphasia, are uncommon, although reductions in fluency may be observed. HIV pathogenic processes can affect any part of the brain; therefore, other patterns are possible. An NCD due to HIV infection can resolve, improve, slowly worsen, or have a fluctuating course. Rapid progression to profound neurocognitive impairment is uncommon in the context of currently available combination antiviral treatment; consequently, an abrupt change in mental status in an individual with HIV may prompt an evaluation of other medical sources for the cognitive change, including secondary infections.

questions.question_text: What is the characteristic gait pattern seen in Huntington's disease?
questions.explanation: Huntington's disease is characterized by a lurching, chaotic gait pattern, distinct from the scissoring gait of upper motor neuron lesions or the broad, unsteady gait of cerebellar disease.

questions.question_text: You are seeing a 75yearold female patient with major neurocognitive disorder, diminished reflexes, poor proprioception, dysesthesia, and anemia. Which of the following abnormal lab values is likely to reveal the cause of these symptoms?
questions.explanation: Vitamin B12 (cobalamin) deficiency is characterized by cognitive impairment, hyporeflexia, subacute combined degeneration of the spinal cord (leading to limited proprioception), and megaloblastic anemia (with elevated mean corpuscular volume) and in severe cases can mimic dementia. However, elevation in methylmalonic acid levels is more directly correlated with functional B12 deficiency. Vitamin B1 (thiamine) deficiency leads to Wernicke– Korsakoff syndrome, as well as dry beriberi (neuropathy) and wet beriberi (cardiomyopathy). Vitamin B3 (niacin) deficiency is characterized by diarrhea and dermatitis. Vitamin B6 (pyridoxine) deficiency is characterized by seborrheic dermatitis, glossitis, and somnolence. Vitamin C deficiency (scurvy) is characterized by fatigue, easy bruising, bleeding diathesis, and extrapyramidal symptoms. Vitamin E deficiency is rare and characterized by several neurological deficits (retinopathy, dysarthria, loss of deep tendon reflexes, poor proprioception) but does not cause cognitive issues. 11. tREAtmENt OF NEUROPS

questions.question_text: What is the most common feature of Wernicke's aphasia?
questions.explanation: Wernicke's aphasia is characterized by fluent but unintelligible speech often called jargon aphasia or word salad, with poor auditory comprehension despite relatively fluent output.

questions.question_text: DIAGNOStIC AND C LINICAL EvALUAt
questions.explanation: Sydenham chorea is seen most frequently in girls who have a history of Group A betahemolytic streptococcal infection/ rheumatic fever and is characterized by irregular movements of the limbs, trunk, and face. Movements occur as a result of autoantibodies attacking the basal ganglia. Most children recover. Pediatric acuteonset neuropsychiatric syndrome (PANS; until recently known as pediatric autoimmune neuropsychiatric disorder associated with streptococcal infection, or PANDAS) is also a disorder associated with Group A betahemolytic streptococcal infection; however, PANS is associated with onset of vocal and/ or motor tics. Tics in Tourette syndrome can usually be suppressed with effort and are stereotyped rather than irregular.

questions.question_text: A 9-year-old girl presents with an acute onset of irregular involuntary movements of her limbs, trunk, and face, along with new-onset obsessive-compulsive symptoms, following a throat infection. Her throat swab is positive for Group A beta-haemolytic Streptococcus. Which of the following best describes the pathophysiological mechanism underlying her neuropsychiatric symptoms?

options.text: Autoantibodies directed against the basal ganglia
Direct bacterial invasion of the central nervous system
Vasculitis of the middle cerebral artery

correct_answer.text: Autoantibodies directed against the basal ganglia

questions.explanation: Sydenham\'s chorea results from an autoimmune response to Group A beta-haemolytic Streptococcus infection in which autoantibodies cross-react with and attack the basal ganglia (particularly the caudate nucleus), producing involuntary choreiform movements and obsessive-compulsive symptoms; this immunopathological mechanism also underlies PANDAS (Paediatric Autoimmune Neuropsychiatric Disorders Associated with Streptococcal infections).PANDAS is thought to be secondary to streptococcal infection and mediated by autoantibodies binding to basal ganglia,\' and the New Oxford Textbook of Psychiatry (p.806) notes that OCD symptoms occur in over 70% of Sydenham\'s chorea cases with antibodies directed against the caudate. Option B (cerebellum) is incorrect as the target structure is the basal ganglia, not cerebellum. Option C (direct bacterial invasion of the CNS) is incorrect as the mechanism is immune-mediated rather than infective. Option D (demyelination of corticospinal tracts) is a feature of demyelinating diseases such as multiple sclerosis and is not relevant here. Option E (vasculitis of the middle cerebral artery) describes a vascular mechanism unrelated to GABHS-associated autoimmune neuropsychiatric disorders.

questions.question_text: In which condition is bilateral FLAIR hyperintensities of the posterior thalamic nucleus seen?
questions.explanation: Bilateral FLAIR hyperintensities of the posterior thalamic nucleus, known as the pulvinar sign, is a characteristic finding in variant CJD. While the pulvinar sign can also be seen in status epilepticus, ADEM, and bilateral thalamic infarcts, it is most classically associated with variant CJD.

questions.question_text: Ideational apraxia is characterized by:

options.text: Inability to make fine delicate movements
Inability to follow learned tasks when given objects
Inability to perform actions in correct sequence
Inability to copy pictures or combine parts

correct_answer.text: Inability to perform actions in correct sequence

questions.explanation: Ideational apraxia involves inability to perform actions in the correct sequence; patients can perform individual actions but cannot perform them in proper order, and can obey single commands.

questions.question_text: Which is NOT a type of frontotemporal dementia?
questions.explanation: Progressive supranuclear palsy (PSP) is a distinct tauopathy but is not classified as a type of frontotemporal dementia; it is a separate parkinsonian disorder.

questions.question_text: Dementia and Parkinsonism A patient presents with dementia and parkinsonian features including rigidity and bradykinesia. Which condition is associated with both dementia and parkinsonism?

options.text: All of the above can present with both

correct_answer.text: All of the above can present with both

questions.explanation: Multiple dementias can present with parkinsonism: PDD, DLB, vascular dementia, corticobasal degeneration, and even advanced Alzheimer's.

questions.question_text: Among the following options, which is expected in the cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) in a individual with herpes simplex virus (HSV) encephalitis? tION OF N EUROLOGICAL DISORDERS • 141

options.text: Normal protein level with white blood cells
Normal glucose with white blood cells only
Elevated lymphocyte count with red blood cells
Elevated glucose and normal lymphocyte count
Markedly decreased protein level with decreased glucose

correct_answer.text: Elevated lymphocyte count with red blood cells

questions.explanation: In aseptic encephalitis, CSF reveals increased lymphocyte count, often with red blood cells with or without xanthochromia. The prefix “xantho” means yellow, and this color is due to breakdown of red blood cells in CSF. Protein levels may be mildly raised, and glucose will be normal or mildly decreased.

questions.question_text: In HIV-associated neurocognitive disorder in a patient on long-term ART, which finding would be expected?
questions.explanation: Even with successful ART and high CD4 counts, neuronal loss and cognitive impairment can persist due to chronic neuroinflammation and viral remnants.

questions.question_text: A 17yearold male is hit on the left side of his head with a line drive while playing baseball. He collapses Y BOARD REvIEw with significant head pain but is able to get up and go home without any discomfort. Over the next hour he becomes more somnolent, and his headache worsens. Which of the following would explain this presentation?
questions.explanation: The above scenario likely represents a case of epidural hematoma. The epidural hematoma results from temporal bone injury with laceration of the middle meningeal artery. This is essentially a rapidly expanding, highpressure blood clot, which can compress the underlying brain and produce transtentorial herniation. Individuals with epidural hematoma may regain consciousness for a short while after initial insult before they lapse into coma. This brief period of consciousness is called the lucid interval.

questions.question_text: Among the following, which is not a feature of Stage I Alzheimer’s dementia?
questions.explanation: According to Cummings, Alzheimer’s disease progresses through three stages. In the fi rst stage, the patient has anomia, defective visuospatial skills and calculation ability along with an indifferent personality. Examination of the motor system and EEG may be relatively normal, although some medial temporal atrophy may be noted in a structural brain scan. In the second stage of dementia, the patient has fl uent aphasia and further deterioration in memory, visuospatial skills, and personality. In addition, there may be motor restlessness on examination. EEG may show background slowing and a structural brain scan may show temperoparietal atrophy. In the third and fi nal stage, there is severe impairment in intellectual function and speech disturbances characterized by palilalia, echolalia, or mutism. In addition, there is sphincter disturbances, diffuse slowing on EEG and diffuse atrophy on structural scan. Cummings JL and Mega MS. Neuropsychiatry and Behavioural Neuroscience, 2nd edn. Oxford University Press, 2003, p. 148.

questions.question_text: MCI vs Dementia - Best Discriminator A patient may have mild cognitive impairment or early dementia. You want to differentiate between them. Which assessment best discriminates MCI from dementia?
questions.explanation: The key difference is preserved daily functioning in MCI vs impaired ADLs in dementia. Informant-based functional assessment is most sensitive.

questions.question_text: A 17yearold female comes to her primary care doctor to evaluate headache. She reports that in the past year she has had six episodes of severe throbbing pain on the left side of her head. She has associated nausea and sensitivity to light. These symptoms are most consistent with which of the following?
questions.explanation: Migraine headache is classified by at least five attacks lasting 4 to 72 hours (untreated) with two of the following: unilateral location, pulsating quality, moderate or severe pain intensity, or aggravation by or avoidance of physical activity; and also with one of the following: nausea/ vomiting or photophobia/ phonophobia. Symptoms are not better accounted for by another diagnosis.

questions.question_text: Coiled bodies are pathological inclusions characteristically seen in which condition?
questions.explanation: Coiled bodies are neurofibrillary tangles and tau inclusions found in astrocytes and oligodendrocytes, particularly in the substantia nigra, subthalamic nucleus, and globus pallidus. These are characteristic microscopic findings in progressive supranuclear palsy, a rare disorder affecting gait, balance, mood, and cognition.

questions.question_text: Wernicke's aphasia
questions.explanation: Wernicke's aphasia is characterized by fluent speech but with poor comprehension (receptive language impairment), in contrast to Broca's aphasia which is non-fluent and expressive.

questions.question_text: Which organism is implicated in the development of OCD?
questions.explanation: Patients with OCD, Tourette syndrome, or tic disorders were more likely than controls to have had prior streptococcal infection. The risk was higher among children with multiple streptococcal infections within 12 months. Group A beta-hemolytic streptococcal infection is implicated in the pathogenesis of OCD.

questions.question_text: Seizures originating from the parietal lobe typically begin with which type of aura?
questions.explanation: Parietal lobe seizures typically begin with a contralateral somatosensory sensation, usually of the positive type such as electrical sensations or tingling.

questions.question_text: Locked-in syndrome resulting from a ventral pontine lesion is characterized by:

options.text: Complete inability to move or communicate
Preserved eye movements and ability to open eyes, with loss of horizontal eye movements and other voluntary movement

correct_answer.text: Preserved eye movements and ability to open eyes, with loss of horizontal eye movements and other voluntary movement

questions.explanation: Locked-in syndrome from ventral pontine lesion results in total paralysis below the third nerve nuclei, but patients can open eyes voluntarily and elevate/depress eyes to command, while horizontal eye movements are usually lost.

questions.question_text: Factors affecting the presence of neuropsychiatric symptoms in head tumours include

options.text: Location relative to eloquent brain areas

questions.explanation: The anatomical location of a tumour is an important factor that predicts the development of neuropsychiatric problems in the population. For example, left temporal lobe tumours are most commonly associated with psychosis. To some extent, the symptoms represent the underlying function of the involved lobe. The aggressiveness of the tumour itself and the rapidity and extent of its spread are also believed to be important factors in the type, acuity, and severity of psychiatric and behavioural symptoms that may be associated with it. Thus, rapidly growing tumours are frequently associated with more acute psychiatric symptomatology, as well as signifi cant neurocognitive impairment. In this case, raised intracranial tension is associated with rapid growth and hence more behavioural problems. In general, the specifi c histological characteristics of brain tumours have not been shown to be correlated with specifi c psychiatric and behavioural symptoms. However, as noted previously, more aggressive tumours, such as high- grade gliomas, are more likely to be associated with acute psychiatric and behavioural symptoms than are slower growing malignant and benign tumours. Kaplan HI. Kaplan and Sadock’s Comprehensive Textbook of Psychiatry, 8th ed. Lippincott Williams and Wilkins, 2004, p. 363.

questions.question_text: A 34-year-old man with poorly controlled HIV (CD4 count 80 cells/μL) presents with headache, confusion, and fever. CT brain shows multiple ring-enhancing lesions with surrounding edema. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Toxoplasmosis causes multiple ring-enhancing lesions in HIV patients with low CD4 counts.

questions.question_text: Reversible Dementia A clinician reviews causes of cognitive impairment that may be reversible. Which dementia type has the most potential for improvement with abstinence?
questions.explanation: Alcohol-related cognitive impairment may partially improve with abstinence and nutrition (thiamine). Other dementias are progressive.

questions.question_text: A 68yearold male patient with an extensive smoking history exhibits severe low back pain, numbness and weakness in the lower extremities, and urinary incontinence. In addition, he reports weight loss and hoarseness of voice. What is the next best step in the clinical approach?
questions.explanation: The above case suggests the clinical presentation of epidural cord compression in the context of likely lung malignancy. In 20% of cases, epidural cord compression is the initial presenting symptom of the malignancy. The most important prognostic factors are early diagnosis and early therapeutic intervention. MRI imaging is superior over CT when epidural cord compression is suspected. When cord compression is suspected and MRI is not available, glucocorticoids should be initiated, especially with severe symptom presentation. Early administration of glucocorticoids may increase the likelihood that a patient will be ambulatory at the end of treatment and at 6month follow up. Other modalities, including surgery and external beam radiotherapy, have a role in treatment of cord compression after dexamethasone treatment.

questions.question_text: Confabulation is best described as which of the following?

options.text: Can only occur in Korsakoff syndrome
Always involves deliberate falsification of facts
A falsification of memory occurring in clear consciousness associated with organic states
Always involves subjective awareness of memory impairment

correct_answer.text: A falsification of memory occurring in clear consciousness associated with organic states

questions.explanation: Confabulation is a falsification of memory occurring in clear consciousness associated with organic states. It is often described in Korsakoff syndrome and can occur in other conditions with clouded consciousness. Autobiographical memory is frequently affected, though not always with subjective awareness.

questions.question_text: Which type of memory is most affected in Korsakoff syndrome?
questions.explanation: Korsakoff syndrome, due to thiamine deficiency, primarily affects episodic memory (memory for specific events), while implicit and procedural memories remain relatively preserved.

questions.question_text: Which of the following are the core clinical features required for diagnosis of Lewy body dementia (need two or more)?

options.text: Memory loss as early feature, rigidity, and visual hallucinations
Spontaneous motor features of Parkinsonism, fluctuating cognition, and recurrent visual hallucinations
Early memory impairment, tremor, and auditory hallucinations
Pyramidal signs, myoclonus, and akinetic mutism
Spasticity, cognitive decline, and behavioral changes

correct_answer.text: Spontaneous motor features of Parkinsonism, fluctuating cognition, and recurrent visual hallucinations

questions.explanation: Lewy body dementia requires two or more of the following features: spontaneous motor features of Parkinsonism, fluctuating cognition with notable variation in attention and alertness, recurrent visual hallucinations (typically well-formed), REM sleep behavior disorder, and progressive cognitive decline (memory loss may not be an early feature).

questions.question_text: All of the options below are risk factors for ischemic stroke with the with the exception ofion of:
questions.explanation: Hypertension, alcohol use disorder, previous TIA, and age greater than 65 are risk factors for ischemic stroke. Other risk factors include heart disease, atrial fibrillation, diabetes mellitus, tobacco use, substance use disorders, and atherosclerosis. Caucasian race is not a risk for stroke, with African Americans more than twice as likely as Caucasians to die of stroke.

questions.question_text: Epileptic automatisms are characteristically described by which feature?
questions.explanation: Epileptic automatisms typically last seconds to minutes and occur during or immediately after seizure activity, distinguishing them from other types of automatisms.

questions.question_text: What is the basis of prion disease?
questions.explanation: Prion diseases such as Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease (CJD) and variant CJD (vCJD) are based on misfolding of the prion protein, leading to accumulation of abnormal protein.

questions.question_text: All of the below options apply factors render a person at high risk for development of post-operative delirium with the exception of
questions.explanation: Along with a number of other factors, including extremes of age, pre-existing cognitive impairment, central nervous system disorders, medical comorbidity, medications, hypothermia, and electrolyte imbalance, hypoalbuminaemia is an important often unnoticed risk factor. Hypoalbuminaemia results in greater bioavailability of many drugs that use albumin as a transporter protein. This leads to greater side-effects resulting in delirium. This may not be picked up by carrying out therapeutic drug monitoring. In addition to the above, a number of surgical factors predispose to delirium, including long duration of operation, emergency procedures, and type of surgery (e.g. hip surgery). Hales RE and Yudofsky SC. The American Psychiatric Publishing Textbook of Neuropsychiatry and Clinical Neurosciences, 4th edn. American Psychiatric Press, 2002, p. 534.

questions.question_text: Mr Cox is a 56-year-old man with chronic schizophrenia, who has been smoking 20 cigarettes a day since his teenage years. On a routine medical examination, it is noted that the BP in his right arm is 184/98, and on the left 155/80. The examination is repeated on several other occasions, and the difference in blood pressure between the arms is found to be consistent. Which artery is most likely to be affected?
questions.explanation: The vignette suggests that the subclavian artery is affected, most likely by atherosclerosis. Discrepancy in left and right arm blood pressures is associated with higher risk of cardiovascular events.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is the most common opportunistic infection of CNS in patients with AIDS?
questions.explanation: Toxoplasmic encephalitis (TE) is caused by the protozoan Toxoplasma gondii. The disease occurs almost exclusively because of reactivation of latent tissue cysts. Primary infection occasionally is associated with acute cerebral or disseminated disease. Seroprevalence varies substantially among different communities (e.g., approximately 15% in the United States and 50%--75% in certain European countries). Prior to the introduction of antiretroviral drugs, the 12-month incidence of TE was approximately 33%. The incidence has decreased substantially with the initiation of ART. Clinical disease is rare among patients with CD4+ T lymphocyte counts more than 200 cells/μL. Primary infection occurs after eating undercooked meat containing tissue cysts or ingestion of oocysts that have been shed in cat feces and have sporulated in the environment (which requires at least 24 hours). No transmission of the organism occurs by person-toperson contact (Retrieved from http://www.cdc.gov/mmwr/preview/mmwrhtml/rr58e324a1.htm).

questions.question_text: Which of the following is a characteristic feature of narcolepsy?
questions.explanation: The cardinal symptoms of narcolepsy include excessive daytime drowsiness with sudden onset of REM sleep, often accompanied by cataplexy (sudden loss of muscle tone, provoked by strong emotion). Sleep paralysis and hypnagogic hallucinations may also occur albeit less commonly.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is a true statement concerning human HIV disease?

options.text: Psychosis is the most common HIV related psychiatric problem.
CSF viral load is the best predictor of HIV related CNS disease.
HIV cross the blood brain barrier using macrophages
CD4 count is the better indicator for severity than viral load

correct_answer.text: HIV cross the blood brain barrier using macrophages

questions.explanation: In order to enter the brain, HIV-1 must cross the BBB using mechanisms that remain unclear. The generally accepted model is the 'Trojan Horse hypothesis'. HIV enters the CNS as a passenger in cells trafficking to the brain via CD4 T cells or monocytes (Retrovirology: HIV-1 associated dementia. Retrieved from http://www.retrovirology.com/content/3/1/28).

questions.question_text: You have noticed some degree of cognitive decline and weight loss in an intravenous drug user. The most probable diagnosis is
questions.explanation: One of the common sources of acquiring HIV infection is intravenous drug use. Subcortical dementia is common in patients with HIV in late stages of their illness

questions.question_text: Mr Edwards is a 60-year-old man who has erectile dysfunction. He attends his GP asking about sildenafil. Which of the following is a common side-effect of this medication?
questions.explanation: The most common side-effects of sildenafil are: headache, flushing, indigestion, nasal congestion, and impaired vision, including photophobia and blurred vision. Some patients have complained of their vision being tinted blue (cyanopsia), or blurriness and loss of peripheral vision.

questions.question_text: A patient with Parkinson's disease experiences visual hallucinations on levodopa/carbidopa therapy. The most appropriate intervention would be to initiate treatment with which of the following medications?
questions.explanation: Atypical antipsychotic, especially quetiapine, have a reduced likelihood of causing adverse drug-induced parkinsonism and therefore a possible role in treating psychotic symptoms in patients with Parkinson's, including the hallucinations induced by levodopa/carbidopa.
